items.stem: A qubit is measured many times and returns 0 about 25% of the time and 1 about 75% of the time. What does this tell you about its state before measurement?

options.text: It was in a superposition whose amplitudes gave probabilities of about 0.25 and 0.75
options.rationale: Correct: measurement probabilities are the squared magnitudes of the amplitudes of the pre-measurement superposition.

options.text: It was definitely 1 and the 0 results are hardware errors
options.rationale: A stable 75/25 split reflects the state's amplitudes, not random hardware error.

options.text: It was both 0 and 1 simultaneously in a classical sense
options.rationale: Superposition is a probability amplitude description, not a classical 'both values' object.

options.text: The qubit had no defined state until the vendor assigned one
options.rationale: The state is defined by its amplitudes; measurement reveals an outcome probabilistically.

items.explanation: Correct: measurement probabilities are the squared magnitudes of the amplitudes of the pre-measurement superposition.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about entanglement are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Measuring one entangled qubit is correlated with the outcome of its partner
options.rationale: Correct: entangled qubits show correlated measurement outcomes.

options.text: Entanglement is a genuinely non-classical resource used by many quantum algorithms
options.rationale: Correct: entanglement has no classical analogue and underlies quantum advantage in several algorithms.

options.text: Entanglement lets you send information faster than light
options.rationale: No usable signal travels faster than light; correlations cannot carry a message on their own.

options.text: Entangled qubits can be freely copied to back them up
options.rationale: The no-cloning theorem forbids copying an unknown quantum state.

items.explanation: Correct: entangled qubits show correlated measurement outcomes.

items.stem: A vendor claims their 50-qubit noisy device already runs deep algorithms that break RSA. What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Current noisy intermediate-scale devices cannot run the deep, error-corrected circuits RSA-breaking requires
options.rationale: Correct: breaking RSA needs far more logical, error-corrected qubits than today's noisy hardware provides.

options.text: Any 50-qubit device can break RSA because 50 qubits exceed RSA key sizes
options.rationale: Qubit count does not map onto key bits that way; error correction and depth dominate.

options.text: RSA is already broken by classical computers so the claim is routine
options.rationale: RSA is not broken classically; this misstates the baseline.

options.text: The claim is plausible because noise improves algorithm accuracy
options.rationale: Noise degrades, not improves, circuit results.

items.explanation: Correct: breaking RSA needs far more logical, error-corrected qubits than today's noisy hardware provides.
